Secrets live in environment variables; commit only `.env.example`

captions.text: Real AI projects are never a single file.
They read prompts and documents from disk, exchange JSON with APIs, and need secret
API keys that must never end up in your code.
This lesson covers all of that.
You will split code into modules and packages, and import between them.
Read and write files safely with pathlib.
Convert between JSON and Python objects, and handle invalid JSON.
And keep configuration and secrets in environment variables.
First, how Python code is organised.
A module is simply a Python file.
Anything defined in cleaning dot py, functions, classes, variables, can be imported
elsewhere.
A package is a folder of modules with a file called dunder init dot py.
That file runs when the package is imported, and it often re-exports the most useful
names.
Your program imports the package by name, exactly like it imports anything else.
And there are two other sources of modules: the standard library, which ships with
Python, like json, pathlib, and os, and third-party packages you install with pip,
like httpx.
Here is the module.
Normalize collapses runs of whitespace by splitting the text into words and joining
them back with single spaces.
And word count reuses normalize.
Small functions that build on each other.
The package's init file imports the two functions, so users can call them directly
on textkit.
And dunder all documents which names are public.
Two import styles.
Import textkit gives you the whole package, used with a prefix.
From textkit dot cleaning import word count brings in a single name.
The main function does the work.
This final check is a Python idiom.
Dunder name equals dunder main is true only when the file is run directly.
If another file imports it, main does not run automatically.
Running main gives the cleaned text and the word count.
And because textkit is a proper package, any other code in this folder can import it
too.
If you see module not found error for your own package, you are almost always
running Python from the wrong folder.
Python looks for imports starting in the folder of the script you run.
Run from the project root, and for packages, use python dash m.
Next, files.
Prompts, documents, logs, and reports all live in files.
The modern way to work with them is pathlib.
A Path object represents a file path.
Write text creates or overwrites the file.
Always pass encoding equals utf eight.
The default encoding is different on Windows, and AI text is full of characters
outside basic English.
Read text returns the whole file as one string, and splitlines turns it into a list
of lines.
For more control, open the file inside a with block.
The mode a means append, so we add to the end.
The with statement guarantees the file is closed, even if something fails.
Finally, number the lines, and ask the path a few questions: does it exist, what is
its suffix, and how many bytes is it.
Two lines written, a third appended, and the file is thirty-four bytes.
JSON is a text format for data, and it is everywhere in AI engineering.
Model APIs send and receive JSON, tool calls are described in JSON, and logs are
often JSON.
JSON looks very similar to Python.
Objects in curly braces, arrays in square brackets, strings, numbers, true, false,
and null.
Python's json module maps them directly.
Objects become dictionaries, arrays become lists, and true, false, and null become
True, False, and None.
But JSON is stricter than Python.
Strings need double quotes, and trailing commas are not allowed.
We start from an ordinary Python dictionary.
json dot dumps, with an s for string, converts Python into JSON text.
Indent two makes it readable.
Then we save it to a file.
json dot loads does the reverse, turning JSON text back into Python objects, so the
tokens are a real number again.
And invalid JSON raises a JSON decode error.
Here, a trailing comma.
Language models sometimes produce slightly broken JSON, so you will handle this
error a lot.
Notice true and null in the JSON text, the token count plus one, and the precise
error message, which even tells you the column.
Environment variables keep secrets out of your code.
An API key written in a source file ends up in git history, in screenshots, and in
logs.
They also let settings change without editing code, such as a different model on
your laptop and in production.
And every platform supports them: your terminal, Docker, cloud hosts, and CI
pipelines.
You'll use them all the way to Module 17.
The os module exposes environment variables as a dictionary-like object called
environ.
Get returns None if the variable isn't set, or a default you choose.
If the key is missing, say so clearly instead of failing later in a confusing way.
And never print the secret itself.
Printing its length is enough to confirm it loaded.
With nothing set, the script refuses to continue and uses the default model.
On macOS or Linux, you can set variables for a single command like this.
This is a fake key, just for the demo.
On Windows PowerShell, you'd first run dollar env, colon, DEMO API KEY, equals, and
the value in quotes.
Typing variables every time gets tedious, so projects keep them in a file called dot
env.
You commit a template called dot env dot example, with fake values, so others know
what to set.
The real dot env file holds your actual keys, and it is listed in dot gitignore, so
git never records it.
In the project, we'll write a tiny loader that reads dot env into the environment.
Real variables always win over the file.
Quick check.
Which call turns this JSON text into a Python dictionary?
json dot loads.
The s stands for string.
Dumps goes the other way, and load without an s reads from an open file object.
A module is a file, and a package is a folder with a dunder init file.
Use pathlib, and always set the encoding to utf eight.
Convert with json loads and dumps, and catch JSON decode errors.
Secrets live in environment variables, and only the example file is committed.
In the next lesson, you'll add type hints, talk to web APIs over HTTP, and see why
async makes AI apps faster.
